title: Ludi. Certamen pedum et pugilum
titleEn: The Foot Race and the Boxer's Challenge — Aeneid V.286–386
part: The Foot Race and the Boxer's Challenge (V.286–386)
about: The games go on from the sea to the land. Aeneas leads the crowd to a grassy plain ringed by wooded hills, sits among them, and calls for runners; the Trojans and Sicilians gather, Nisus and Euryalus first, the one beautiful in his green youth and the other loving him with a loyal love. Aeneas announces a prize for every runner, and three for the first three home: a horse, an Amazon's quiver, a Greek helmet. Nisus leads the race, then slips, near the finish, in the blood of the sacrificed bullocks; as he falls he trips Salius, who is just behind, and so puts his friend Euryalus in front. Salius protests, Euryalus has the crowd's sympathy, and Aeneas settles the quarrel by giving Salius a lion's hide and Nisus, who makes a comic show of his filthy limbs, a splendid shield. The fall in the dung and the tripping of a rival come from the foot race of Iliad XXIII, where Ajax slips and Odysseus, helped by Athena, wins. Aeneas then calls for boxers. Dares, who once beat down Butes at Hector's tomb, struts about alone; no one will face him, and he takes the prize bull by the horn and claims it. The Trojans clamour for the promised prize to be given him.

sentences.t:
Hoc pius Aeneas misso certamine tendit
gramineum in campum, quem collibus undique curvis
cingebant silvae, mediaque in valle theatri
circus erat;
sentences.l:
To this, pious Aeneas, the contest dismissed, makes his way,
grassy, into a plain, which with hills on every side curving
were ringing woods, and in the middle valley of a theatre
a circle there was;
sentences.i: After this, devout Aeneas, the contest done, makes for a grassy plain, which woods on the all-round curving hills enclosed; and in the valley's midst there lay a ring of ground like a theatre;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Hoc' looks back to the end of the race: 'after this'. 'Misso certamine' is an ablative absolute, 'the contest being dismissed' ('mitto'), and 'tendit… in campum' is 'makes his way into the plain'. 'Quem' is the object of 'cingebant', 'ringed it'; 'collibus… curvis' is an ablative of place for the curving hills on which the woods stand. In 'mediaque in valle' the 'que' stands after the first word of the phrase, not before the preposition, as often in verse ('and in the middle valley'). 'Theatri circus': the level ring of ground in the valley makes a natural theatre, with the slopes for seats.

sentences.t:
quo se multis cum milibus heros
consessu medium tulit exstructoque resedit.
sentences.l:
to where with many thousands the hero himself
to the middle of the gathering carried himself, and on the built-up seat sat down.
sentences.i: There the hero made his way into the midst of the gathering, with many thousands about him, and sat down on the seat that had been raised for him.
sentences.n: 'Quo' is a connecting adverb, 'to which place'. 'Se… tulit' is the common idiom 'carried himself', that is, 'went'. 'Consessu' is an ablative of place where, 'in the gathering'; 'medium' agrees with the subject, 'heros', 'in the middle of the crowd'. 'Exstructo' is the perfect participle of 'exstruo', 'build up', here a raised seat or platform. 'Resedit' is the perfect of 'resido', 'sat down'. 'Milibus' is the ablative plural of 'mille' as a noun, 'with many thousands'.

sentences.t:
Hic, qui forte velint rapido contendere cursu,
invitat pretiis animos, et praemia ponit.
sentences.l:
Here, those who by chance may wish to contend in swift running,
he invites with prizes in spirit, and rewards sets out.
sentences.i: Here he calls on any who may care to race in a swift run, tempting their hearts with prizes, and he sets the awards out where all can see.
sentences.n: 'Hic' is the adverb 'here', 'at this point'. 'Qui… velint' is a relative clause with the subjunctive, in the sense 'any who may wish'; its antecedent ('eos', 'those') is left out and 'animos' stands for the persons whose spirits he invites. 'Rapido cursu' is an ablative of manner. 'Pretiis' is an ablative of means; 'praemia ponit' is 'sets out the prizes', as at the start of a competition.

sentences.t:
Undique conveniunt Teucri mixtique Sicani,
Nisus et Euryalus primi,
Euryalus forma insignis viridique iuventa,
Nisus amore pio pueri;
sentences.l:
From all sides gather Teucrians and the mingled Sicilians,
Nisus and Euryalus first,
Euryalus by beauty distinguished and green youth,
Nisus by dutiful love of the boy;
sentences.i: From every side they gather, Trojans and the Sicilians mingled with them, Nisus and Euryalus first of all, Euryalus marked out by his beauty and his green youth, Nisus by his loyal love for the lad;
sentences.n: Nisus and Euryalus, the two friends, are introduced here; their story is taken up again in a later book. 'Teucri' are the Trojans (from Teucer, an early king of Troy); 'mixti Sicani' are the Sicilians, the old inhabitants of the island, here mixed in with the Trojans. Line 294, 'Nisus et Euryalus primi,', is a half-line: Virgil left about fifty-eight lines in the poem unfinished, and Greenough prints this one short; the sense is complete. 'Primi' is in apposition to the pair. 'Forma… iuventa' are ablatives of respect with 'insignis'; 'viridi' is 'green', that is, fresh. 'Nisus amore pio' repeats 'insignis' by zeugma, 'Nisus (marked out) by loyal love', and 'pueri' is an objective genitive, 'love for the boy'.

sentences.t:
quos deinde secutus
regius egregia Priami de stirpe Diores;
sentences.l:
whom next following
royal, from the outstanding stock of Priam, Diores;
sentences.i: next after them came Diores, a prince, sprung from Priam's noble line;
sentences.n: 'Quos' is a connecting relative, 'and them', object of 'secutus', the perfect participle of the deponent 'sequor', with 'est' left out: 'Diores followed them'. 'Regius' is 'of royal blood', and 'de stirpe Priami' 'from the stock of Priam' with 'egregia' put between to frame the line. 'Diores' is a Greek form of name.

sentences.t:
hunc Salius simul et Patron, quorum alter Acarnan,
alter ab Arcadio Tegeaeae sanguine gentis;
sentences.l:
him Salius together and Patron, of whom the one an Acarnanian,
the other from the Arcadian blood of the Tegean race;
sentences.i: then Salius and Patron together, one of them an Acarnanian, the other of Arcadian blood, from Tegea's people;
sentences.n: 'Hunc' is Diores, accusative; a verb of following ('secuti sunt') is supplied from the line before. 'Simul et' joins the two names, 'both together'. 'Quorum alter… alter' is 'of whom the one… the other'. 'Acarnan' is a Greek nominative ('Acarnas'), a man from Acarnania in north-west Greece. 'Tegeaeae' agrees with 'gentis': Tegea was a city of Arcadia; 'ab Arcadio sanguine' is 'from Arcadian blood'.

sentences.t:
tum duo Trinacrii iuvenes, Helymus Panopesque,
adsueti silvis, comites senioris Acestae;
sentences.l:
then two Trinacrian youths, Helymus and Panopes,
accustomed to the woods, companions of the elder Acestes;
sentences.i: then two young Sicilians, Helymus and Panopes, at home in the forests and companions of aged Acestes;
sentences.n: 'Trinacrii' is 'of Trinacria', a Greek name for Sicily ('three-cornered'). 'Panopes' is a Greek nominative, with 'que' attached. 'Adsueti' is the perfect participle of 'adsuesco' with the dative, 'accustomed to the woods'. 'Senioris' is a comparative used without a comparison, 'rather old', 'the elder'. 'Acestae' is the genitive of the Greek name Acestes, spelled in the first-declension way.

sentences.t: multi praeterea, quos fama obscura recondit.
sentences.l: many besides, whom an obscure report buries away.
sentences.i: and many others besides, whom an obscure fame keeps hidden away.
sentences.n: 'Multi' is the subject of an understood 'conveniunt', as the list ends. 'Quos' refers back to 'multi'. 'Fama obscura' is 'a dim report'; 'recondit' (from 'recondo') is 'stows away', 'hides': these are too little known to be named, and the poet names only the few.

sentences.t: Aeneas quibus in mediis sic deinde locutus:
sentences.l: Aeneas, in the midst of whom thus next having spoken:
sentences.i: In the midst of these Aeneas then spoke, and spoke thus:
sentences.n: 'Quibus in mediis' is 'in the midst of whom', a connecting relative with its preposition placed between the pronoun and the noun, an ordering you will meet again. 'Locutus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'loquor', with 'est' omitted. The colon announces the speech that follows.

sentences.t: “Accipite haec animis, laetasque advertite mentes:
sentences.l: “Take these things to heart, and, glad, turn your minds:
sentences.i: “Take what I say to heart, and turn glad minds to it:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the opening mark of Aeneas's speech, which runs to 314. 'Accipite' is an imperative; 'animis' is an ablative of place where, 'in your minds'. 'Advertite mentes' is a variant of the usual 'animum advertere', 'turn the mind to', that is, 'pay attention'; 'laetas' agrees with 'mentes'.

sentences.t: nemo ex hoc numero mihi non donatus abibit.
sentences.l: no one out of this number by me not given a gift will depart.
sentences.i: No one in this company shall leave without a gift from me.
sentences.n: 'Nemo… non' is a double negative that means 'everyone' ('there will be no one who will not be given'). 'Donatus' is the perfect participle of 'dono', 'present with a gift', here in the sense 'not having been given a gift'. 'Mihi' is a dative of the agent with a perfect participle ('by me'). 'Ex hoc numero' is 'out of this number'. 'Abibit' is a future.

sentences.t:
Gnosia bina dabo levato lucida ferro
spicula caelatamque argento ferre bipennem;
sentences.l:
Cnossian, two each, I shall give, bright with polished iron,
spear-points, and to carry an axe engraved with silver;
sentences.i: To each I shall give two bright Cretan spearheads with burnished iron, and an axe to carry, chased with silver;
sentences.n: 'Gnosia' is 'of Cnossus', and so 'Cretan' (the Latin Library prints 'Cnosia'); the Cretans were famous archers and iron-workers. 'Bina' is the distributive, 'two apiece'. 'Levato ferro' is an ablative of quality, with 'levato' from 'levo', 'make smooth', here 'polished', not 'lifted'. 'Lucida' agrees with 'spicula' (neuter plural, 'spear-points'). 'Ferre' is an infinitive of purpose after 'dabo' (a poetic construction), and 'caelatam argento' means 'chased (engraved) with silver'. 'Bipennem' is the accusative of 'bipennis', a double-headed axe.

sentences.t: omnibus hic erit unus honos.
sentences.l: to all this shall be one honour.
sentences.i: This is the single honour for all.
sentences.n: 'Hic' agrees with 'honos' and points to the gifts just named. 'Unus' means 'one and the same'. 'Omnibus' is a dative: 'there shall be for all'.

sentences.t:
Tres praemia primi
accipient flavaque caput nectentur oliva.
sentences.l:
Three, the first ones, shall receive prizes,
and their head be wreathed with yellow olive.
sentences.i: The first three to finish will take prizes, and bind their brows in pale olive.
sentences.n: 'Tres… primi' is 'the first three'. 'Caput nectentur' is a passive with an accusative of respect, 'will be bound as to the head' (the poets keep the accusative of the part affected). 'Flava' is 'yellow', 'golden'; 'oliva' is an ablative of means. The olive wreath is the winner's mark.

sentences.t: Primus equum phaleris insignem victor habeto;
sentences.l: The first, as victor, a horse with trappings distinguished let him have;
sentences.i: Let the first man home keep a horse resplendent in its trappings;
sentences.n: 'Habeto' is a future imperative (the -to form), used for formal orders and rules; 'abito' at 314 is the same. 'Phaleris' is the ablative of 'phalerae', the metal discs on a horse's harness; the ablative goes with 'insignem', 'distinguished by'. 'Victor' is in apposition to 'primus', 'as victor'.

sentences.i: the second, an Amazon's quiver, filled with Thracian arrows, circled about with a broad band of gold and clasped beneath with a smooth round jewel;
sentences.n: 'Alter' is 'the second' of the three (the word is used for the second in a series). The verb 'habeto' is understood. 'Plenamque' ('que' joins 'pharetram' and 'plenam') is 'and full'. 'Threïciis' is spelled with a diaeresis to show it has three syllables. 'Quam circum' puts the preposition after its pronoun; 'balteus' is the belt and the subject of 'amplectitur', 'embraces with broad gold' ('lato auro'). 'Fibula' is the subject of 'subnectit', the clasp 'fastens it from beneath'; 'tereti gemma' is 'with a rounded gem'. The Thracians had a name as archers; the Amazons are the women warriors of legend.

sentences.t: tertius Argolica hac galea contentus abito.”
sentences.l: the third, with this Argive helmet content, let him depart.”
sentences.i: and the third go off content with this Greek helmet.”
sentences.n: 'Hac' points at the helmet: Aeneas is holding it up. 'Argolica' is 'of Argos', that is, Greek. 'Contentus' takes the ablative, 'content with'. 'Abito' is a future imperative. The closing mark ends the speech.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi dicta, locum capiunt, signoque repente
corripiunt spatia audito, limenque relinquunt,
effusi nimbo similes, simul ultima signant.
sentences.l:
These things when said, their place they take, and at the signal suddenly
seize the course, once heard, and the starting-line leave,
poured out like a rain-cloud, together the farthest marks they eye.
sentences.i: When this was said, they took their places, and, the signal sounding, all at once seized the track and left the line, streaming out like a rain-cloud, all marking the far goal together.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Haec ubi dicta' is 'when these things (were) said', with 'sunt' left out. 'Locum capiunt' is 'take their place' on the starting-line. 'Signoque… audito' is an ablative absolute, with 'repente' wedged between its two words. 'Corripiunt spatia' is 'snatch up the ground', 'seize the track'; 'limen' is the threshold, here the starting-line. 'Effusi' is the perfect participle of 'effundo', 'poured out', and 'nimbo' is a dative with 'similes' ('like'). 'Ultima signant' is 'mark the farthest (things)', fixing their eyes and minds on the goal. The scene is closely built on the foot race of Iliad XXIII, where the runners also 'pour' away from the line.

sentences.t:
Primus abit longeque ante omnia corpora Nisus
emicat, et ventis et fulminis ocior alis;
sentences.l:
First goes off, and far before all bodies, Nisus
darts out, both than winds and than lightning's wings swifter;
sentences.i: Nisus is away first, and shoots far ahead of every other runner, swifter than the winds and than the wings of the lightning;
sentences.n: 'Primus' agrees with 'Nisus', held back to the end of the second line; 'emicat' (from 'emico') is 'flashes out', 'darts forth'. 'Ante omnia corpora' is 'before all the bodies', the other runners. 'Ocior' is a comparative, with 'ventis' and 'fulminis… alis' as two ablatives of comparison, joined by 'et… et'.

sentences.t:
proximus huic, longo sed proxumus intervallo,
insequitur Salius;
sentences.l:
Nearest to him, but nearest by a long interval,
follows Salius;
sentences.i: Next to him comes Salius, though next only by a wide gap;
sentences.n: 'Proximus' (Greenough prints the second one, 'proxumus', with the old -umus spelling, as in 'maxumus') is 'nearest'; 'huic' is a dative with it. The repetition with 'sed' is a concession: next, yes, but only just in order. 'Longo… intervallo' is an ablative of the degree of difference, 'by a long interval'. 'Insequitur' is 'follows close'.

sentences.t:
spatio post deinde relicto
tertius Euryalus:
sentences.l:
with a space afterwards then left,
third Euryalus:
sentences.i: then, with a gap left behind him, third comes Euryalus;
sentences.n: 'Spatio… relicto' is an ablative absolute, 'a space having been left' (between Salius and the next). The verb is left out ('sequitur' or 'est' to be supplied from 'insequitur'). Line 322 is a half-line: Greenough prints 'tertius Euryalus:' short, and the sense is complete. The colon leads on to the runner behind.

sentences.t: Euryalumque Helymus sequitur;
sentences.l: And Euryalus Helymus follows;
sentences.i: and behind Euryalus follows Helymus;
sentences.n: 'Euryalum' is the object of 'sequitur' (the deponent 'sequor' takes the accusative). The 'que' joins the clause to the one before, and the order of the runners is called out name by name.

sentences.t:
quo deinde sub ipso
ecce volat calcemque terit iam calce Diores,
incumbens umero, spatia et si plura supersint,
transeat elapsus prior, ambiguumque relinquat.
sentences.l:
and right behind him, next,
lo he flies, and heel with now heel treads, Diores,
leaning on shoulder, and, if more spaces were to remain,
might pass, slipping forward, and leave it doubtful.
sentences.i: and close on his heels, see, Diores flies along, treading heel on heel and leaning on his shoulder; and had more ground been left he might have slipped past him in front, or at least have left the matter in doubt.
sentences.n: 'Quo' is a connecting relative, 'and him', Helymus; 'sub ipso' is 'right under him', that is, 'close behind'. 'Ecce volat' is vivid: 'see, he flies'. 'Calcemque terit calce' is 'treads heel with heel', trampling on the other's heel. 'Incumbens' ('lean upon') takes 'umero', usually read as a dative: Diores is pressing on Helymus's shoulder. 'Spatia et si plura supersint' is 'et si plura spatia supersint' with the noun moved forward; 'supersint' and 'transeat' are present subjunctives, a condition less vivid, 'if more room were to remain, he might pass'. 'Elapsus' is the perfect participle of 'elabor', 'having slipped out (from behind)'; 'prior' is a predicate, 'ahead'. 'Ambiguum' is a neuter noun, 'a doubtful matter', and 'ambiguumque' perhaps means 'or at least'.

sentences.t:
Iamque fere spatio extremo fessique sub ipsam
finem adventabant, levi cum sanguine Nisus
labitur infelix, caesis ut forte iuvencis
fusus humum viridisque super madefecerat herbas.
sentences.l:
And now almost on the last stretch and weary, close upon the very
end they were approaching, when on slippery blood Nisus
slips, unlucky, as by chance, the bullocks having been slain,
poured on the ground, it had soaked also over the green grass.
sentences.i: Already, on the last stretch of the track, and weary, they were closing on the very finish, when Nisus, luckless man, slides on slippery blood, which, as it happened, had been spilled when the bullocks were slaughtered and had soaked the ground and the green grass above it.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Iam fere spatio extremo' is 'now almost at the last stretch', an ablative of place. 'Fessi' is the runners; 'adventabant' ('adventare', frequentative of 'advenio') is 'were drawing near'; 'sub ipsam finem' is 'right up to the very end', where 'finis' is feminine, as often in Virgil. 'Cum… labitur' is the 'inverse cum', with the main action in the cum-clause. 'Levi… sanguine' is an ablative of means with 'labitur' ('glides', 'slips'); 'levis' is 'smooth', 'slippery'. 'Infelix' is predicative. In 'caesis ut forte iuvencis fusus humum… madefecerat herbas', 'fusus' agrees with an understood 'sanguis' (the blood spilled when the bullocks were slain, an ablative absolute); 'humum' is an accusative of the place over which; 'viridisque super herbas' puts the preposition after its noun ('-is' is Greenough's accusative plural), and 'madefecerat' is the pluperfect of 'madefacio', 'had soaked'. The model is Iliad XXIII, where Ajax son of Oileus slips in the dung of the oxen slain for the funeral sacrifice, and Odysseus, helped by Athena, takes the lead.

sentences.t:
Hic iuvenis iam victor ovans vestigia presso
haud tenuit titubata solo, sed pronus in ipso
concidit immundoque fimo sacroque cruore.
sentences.l:
Here the youth, now victor, exulting, his footsteps on the pressed
ground not held, staggering, but headlong in the very
filth fell, and the unclean dung and the sacred blood.
sentences.i: At this the young man, already winning and exulting in it, could not keep his staggering feet on the ground he trod, but fell headlong right in the foul dung and the sacred blood.
sentences.n: 'Ovans' is the present participle of 'ovo', 'exult', and 'iam victor' means 'already the winner'. 'Titubata' is the perfect participle of 'titubo' ('stagger'), used with passive form though 'titubo' is intransitive: 'staggered steps' ('vestigia'); 'presso solo' is an ablative, 'on the ground pressed (by his feet)'. 'Pronus' is 'headlong'. 'In ipso immundoque fimo sacroque cruore' is 'in the very foul dung and sacred blood' (the double 'que… que', and 'ipso' agrees with 'fimo'); the blood is 'sacred' because it came from a sacrifice.

sentences.t: Non tamen Euryali, non ille oblitus amorum;
sentences.l: Not however of Euryalus, not he forgetful of his loves;
sentences.i: Yet even then he did not forget Euryalus and the love he bore him;
sentences.n: 'Non… non' is anaphora, 'not… not'. 'Oblitus' is the perfect participle of 'obliviscor', which takes the genitive ('Euryali… amorum'), with 'est' omitted. 'Amorum' is the plural 'of the love'. 'Ille' is emphatic: even in his own fall Nisus does not forget his friend.

sentences.t: nam sese opposuit Salio per lubrica surgens;
sentences.l: for himself he set against Salius, through the slippery places rising;
sentences.i: for as he struggled up out of the slime, he threw himself across the path of Salius;
sentences.n: 'Nam' explains the previous line. 'Sese' is an emphatic 'se'; 'opposuit' (from 'oppono') takes a dative, 'Salio'. 'Per lubrica surgens' is 'rising through the slippery (places)', with 'lubrica' a neuter plural used as a noun. In Homer Ajax's fall costs him the race by accident; Virgil's Nisus turns the fall to his friend's profit, a deliberate foul.

sentences.t: ille autem spissa iacuit revolutus harena.
sentences.l: he, however, in the thick sand lay rolled over.
sentences.i: while Salius, tumbled over, lay in the packed sand.
sentences.n: 'Ille' is Salius; 'autem' marks the contrast, 'on the other hand'. 'Spissa… harena' is an ablative of place, 'thick', 'packed' sand. 'Revolutus' is the perfect participle of 'revolvo', 'rolled over'; 'iacuit' is the perfect of 'iaceo', 'lay'.

sentences.t:
Emicat Euryalus, et munere victor amici
prima tenet, plausuque volat fremituque secundo.
sentences.l:
Darts out Euryalus, and by the gift of his friend victor
the first things holds, and with applause flies and with favouring shouting.
sentences.i: Euryalus springs forward, and, a winner by his friend's gift, holds first place, flying on amid applause and favouring shouts.
sentences.n: 'Emicat' repeats the verb of 319: Euryalus now does what Nisus did, taking his place. 'Munere' is an ablative of cause, 'by the favour (service) of his friend'. 'Prima tenet' is 'holds the first (things)', 'first place', with 'prima' a neuter plural. 'Plausuque… fremituque secundo' is a pair of ablatives sharing 'secundo' ('favouring', literally 'following').

sentences.t: Post Helymus subit, et nunc tertia palma Diores.
sentences.l: After, Helymus comes up, and now third prize Diores.
sentences.i: Helymus comes in next, and now Diores takes the third palm.
sentences.n: 'Post' is an adverb, 'afterwards'; 'subit' is 'comes up'. In the second half the verb is left out: Diores is (or has) 'the third palm' (the prize for the third place), with 'palma', 'palm-branch', standing for the victor's prize.

sentences.t:
Hic totum caveae consessum ingentis et ora
prima patrum magnis Salius clamoribus implet,
ereptumque dolo reddi sibi poscit honorem.
sentences.l:
Here the whole gathering of the vast seating-bank and the front
faces of the elders Salius with great shouting fills,
and the honour snatched by a trick to be given back to him demands.
sentences.i: Then Salius fills the whole vast bank of seats with his shouting, and the front rows where the elders sit, and demands that the honour taken from him by a trick be given back.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Hic' is 'at this point'. 'Cavea' is the curved bank of seats of a theatre, and 'consessum' the whole seated assembly; 'ora prima patrum' is 'the foremost faces of the elders' (the old men of rank sit in front). 'Magnis… clamoribus' is an ablative of means. 'Ereptum dolo… honorem' is 'the honour snatched away by a trick', with 'dolo' an ablative of means; 'reddi' (passive) 'be given back' depends on 'poscit', 'demands that it be given back'; 'sibi' is a dative.

sentences.t:
Tutatur favor Euryalum, lacrimaeque decorae,
gratior et pulchro veniens in corpore virtus.
sentences.l:
Defends Euryalus the favour, and the tears becoming,
and more pleasing also, in a beautiful body coming, valour.
sentences.i: The crowd's favour shields Euryalus, and his comely tears, and a courage all the more welcome for coming in a form so fair.
sentences.n: 'Tutatur' is a deponent (from 'tutor', 'protect') in the singular, agreeing with the nearest subject, 'favor', though 'lacrimae' and 'virtus' are also subjects. 'Decorae' is 'becoming'. 'Gratior' is a comparative, 'more pleasing'; 'et' here means 'even', 'also'. 'Veniens in pulchro corpore' is 'coming in a beautiful body'.

sentences.t:
Adiuvat et magna proclamat voce Diores,
qui subiit palmae, frustraque ad praemia venit
ultima, si primi Salio reddentur honores.
sentences.l:
Helps also and with a great voice cries out Diores,
who has come up to the palm, and in vain to the prizes has come
the last, if the first honours to Salius are to be given back.
sentences.i: Diores backs him too, crying out in a great voice, he who has come in for the palm and has come in vain to the last of the prizes if the first honours are restored to Salius.
sentences.n: 'Adiuvat et' is 'also helps' ('et' meaning 'too'). 'Qui subiit palmae' is 'who came up for the palm'; 'palmae', the prize, is probably the dative with 'subiit'. 'Ad praemia… ultima' is 'to the last prizes', the third place. 'Si… reddentur' is a future condition in the more vivid form: 'if the first honours shall be given back'; 'primi honores' are the first prize, the first of the three. 'Salio' is a dative.

sentences.t:
Tum pater Aeneas “Vestra inquit munera vobis
certa manent, pueri, et palmam movet ordine nemo;
sentences.l:
Then father Aeneas “Your gifts, says he, to you
remain sure, boys, and the palm moves from its order nobody;
sentences.i: Then father Aeneas said: “Your prizes stay sure for you, lads, and no one is shifting the palm from its order;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The opening mark comes after 'Aeneas', so the speech begins in mid-line, and 'inquit' ('says he') is dropped into it, as often in Latin. 'Pater' is Aeneas's title as father of his people. 'Vestra… vobis' is a repetition ('your… for you') for emphasis; 'certa' is a predicative adjective, 'sure'; 'manent' is 'remain'. 'Palmam movet ordine' is 'moves the palm from its order', 'ordine' an ablative of separation, where 'ordo' is the order of finishing; 'nemo' is the subject.

sentences.t: me liceat casus misereri insontis amici.”
sentences.l: let it be permitted to me to pity the mishap of an innocent friend.”
sentences.i: Let me be free to pity the mischance of a friend who did no wrong.”
sentences.n: 'Me liceat… misereri' is 'may it be allowed that I pity', an accusative and infinitive as the subject of 'liceat'. 'Misereri', the deponent 'misereor', takes the genitive: 'casus', here a genitive singular ('of the mishap'). The Latin Library prints 'miserari' (which would take the accusative: 'casus' then plural); the sense is the same. 'Insontis' is 'innocent' ('insons'), and 'amici' is Nisus. The closing mark ends the speech.

sentences.t:
Sic fatus, tergum Gaetuli immane leonis
dat Salio, villis onerosum atque unguibus aureis.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, the hide of a Gaetulian huge lion
he gives to Salius, heavy with shaggy hair and with claws golden.
sentences.i: With these words he gives Salius the huge hide of a Gaetulian lion, heavy with its shaggy mane and with claws of gold.
sentences.n: 'Fatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'for', 'speak', with 'est' omitted. 'Tergum' is the back, the pelt (here the whole skin); 'Gaetuli' is 'of Gaetulia', a region of North Africa. 'Immane' agrees with 'tergum'. 'Villis… atque unguibus aureis' are ablatives with 'onerosum' ('heavy with'): 'villi' is the shaggy hair; the claws are gilded. The prize is a consolation, as 'victis' in the next speech will say.

sentences.t:
Hic Nisus, “Si tanta inquit sunt praemia victis,
et te lapsorum miseret, quae munera Niso
digna dabis, primam merui qui laude coronam,
ni me, quae Salium, fortuna inimica tulisset?”
sentences.l:
Here Nisus: “If so great, he says, are the prizes for the beaten,
and you pity the fallen, what gifts to Nisus
worthy will you give, he who the first crown by merit earned,
if me, as Salius, fortune hostile had not carried off?”
sentences.i: At this Nisus: “If prizes so great, he says, fall to the beaten, and you feel for those who fell, what gift will you give Nisus that is worthy of him, who earned the first crown by his running, had not hostile fortune struck me down, as it did Salius?”
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Nisus's speech, again in mid-line, with 'inquit' dropped into the protasis. 'Victis' is a dative. 'Te lapsorum miseret' is the impersonal 'miseret' with the accusative of the person ('te') and the genitive of the cause of pity ('lapsorum', perfect participle of 'labor', 'of those who fell'). 'Niso' is Nisus speaking of himself in the third person, so the relative clause 'qui… merui' takes the first person of the 'ego' behind it. 'Ni… tulisset' is a past condition contrary to fact ('ni', 'nisi'); 'quae Salium' leaves 'tulit' to be supplied ('which carried off Salius'), and 'fortuna' is the subject. There is an irony here: it was Nisus himself who sent Salius sprawling. The closing mark ends the speech.

sentences.t:
Et simul his dictis faciem ostentabat et udo
turpia membra fimo.
sentences.l:
And together with these words his face he displayed and with wet
foul limbs with dung.
sentences.i: And as he spoke he held up for all to see his face, and his limbs, ugly with wet dung.
sentences.n: 'Ostentabat', the imperfect, governs both 'faciem' and 'membra' ('et… et'). 'Udo… fimo' is an ablative of cause or respect with 'turpia', 'foul with wet dung'. 'Simul his dictis' is 'at the same time as these words'.

sentences.t:
Risit pater optimus olli
et clipeum efferri iussit, Didymaonis artem,
Neptuni sacro Danais de poste refixum.
sentences.l:
Laughed the father, best, at him
and a shield to be carried out ordered, Didymaon's work,
from Neptune's sacred doorpost by the Danaans taken down.
sentences.i: The kindly father laughed at him, and bade them bring out a shield, Didymaon's craftsmanship, which the Danaans had torn from the sacred doorpost of Neptune;
sentences.n: 'Olli' is the archaic form of the dative 'illi' ('at him'), used by the old poets; 'rideo' takes the dative. 'Pater optimus' is 'the excellent father', 'the kindest of men'. 'Efferri' is a passive infinitive after 'iussit' ('ordered the shield to be carried out'). 'Didymaonis artem' is an accusative in apposition to 'clipeum', 'the work of Didymaon'; the Latin Library prints the plural 'artes'. 'Refixum' is the perfect participle of 'refigo', 'unfasten', 'take down'; 'Danais' is a dative, probably of the agent (the Danaans had taken it from Neptune's temple). The history of the shield is not told.

sentences.t: Hoc iuvenem egregium praestanti munere donat;
sentences.l: With this the youth excellent with a surpassing gift he presents;
sentences.i: With this outstanding gift he honours the fine young man;
sentences.n: 'Donat' takes the accusative of the person and the ablative of the gift, 'presents him with': 'iuvenem egregium' is Nisus, and 'hoc… praestanti munere' the shield. The semicolon after it closes Greenough's paragraph.

sentences.t: Post, ubi confecti cursus, et dona peregit:
sentences.l: Afterwards, when the races were finished, and the gifts he had completed:
sentences.i: Afterwards, when the races were run and the prizes all given out, he said:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ubi confecti cursus' is 'when the races (were) finished', with 'sunt' left out; 'dona peregit' is 'carried the gifts through', 'went through the prize-giving'. The colon leads into Aeneas's next announcement, which has no 'he said' before it; Latin often lets a colon do that work.

sentences.t:
“Nunc, si cui virtus animusque in pectore praesens,
adsit, et evinctis attollat brachia palmis.”
sentences.l:
“Now, if to anyone valour and spirit in the breast is present,
let him come forward, and, the hands bound, lift his arms.”
sentences.i: “Now, if any man has courage and a ready spirit in his breast, let him step forward, and lift his arms with his hands bound up.”
sentences.n: The marks enclose Aeneas's call for boxers. 'Si cui' is 'si alicui' (after 'si' the 'ali-' drops), 'to anyone', and 'est' is left out. 'Praesens' agrees with 'animus': a spirit 'at hand', ready. 'Adsit' is a jussive subjunctive, 'let him be present', 'let him step forward'. 'Evinctis… palmis' is an ablative absolute, 'the hands having been bound' (with the boxing-straps); 'attollat brachia' is 'raise his arms', the boxer's guard. Greenough spells 'brachia'; the Latin Library 'bracchia'.

sentences.t:
Sic ait, et geminum pugnae proponit honorem,
victori velatum auro vittisque iuvencum,
ensem atque insignem galeam solacia victo.
sentences.i: So he speaks, and sets up a double prize for the fight: a bullock for the winner, dressed in gold and ribbons, and a sword and a splendid helmet to console the man who loses.
sentences.n: 'Ait' is the defective verb 'aio', 'says'. 'Geminum… honorem' is a 'twofold' prize, and 'pugnae' a genitive of the thing it is for. 'Velatum auro vittisque' is 'veiled with gold and fillets', the horns gilded and bound with ribbons, as sacrificial bulls were. 'Ensem atque insignem galeam' stand in apposition to 'solacia', 'as consolations', and 'victo' is a dative, 'for the beaten man'.

sentences.t:
Nec mora: continuo vastis cum viribus effert
ora Dares, magnoque virum se murmure tollit;
sentences.l:
No delay: at once with huge strength lifts
his face Dares, and with great murmur of men raises himself;
sentences.i: No delay: at once Dares lifts his head, huge in his strength, and rises to his feet amid a great murmur from the crowd;
sentences.n: 'Nec mora' is a clipped phrase, 'and no delay'. 'Effert ora' is 'lifts his face'; 'vastis cum viribus' is 'with huge strength'. 'Virum' is the old genitive plural, 'of men' (you will see this constantly: 'divom', 'superum', 'Danaum'); 'magno… murmure' is an ablative of manner, 'se tollit' is 'raises himself'. 'Dares' is a Greek nominative.

sentences.t:
solus qui Paridem solitus contendere contra,
idemque ad tumulum, quo maximus occubat Hector,
victorem Buten immani corpore, qui se
Bebrycia veniens Amyci de gente ferebat,
perculit, et fulva moribundum extendit harena.
sentences.l:
he alone who with Paris was wont to contend face to face,
and the same, at the tomb where greatest Hector lies,
victor Butes, of huge body, who himself
from Bebrycian, coming, of Amycus' race gave out,
struck down, and on the tawny sand the dying stretched out.
sentences.i: he alone who was used to take on Paris, and the same who, beside the mound where mighty Hector lies, struck down the champion Butes, enormous in frame, who gave himself out as sprung from Amycus's Bebrycian stock, and stretched him dying on the tawny sand.
sentences.n: The sentence is long and the verbs wait: 'solus qui… solitus' ('solitus est', from 'soleo', which has a deponent perfect) 'who alone was accustomed'; 'contendere contra' with 'Paridem' put before 'contra' ('contra Paridem'), 'to contend against Paris'. 'Idemque… perculit' is 'and the same man struck down'. 'Quo… occubat Hector' is 'where Hector lies (dead)'. 'Victorem Buten' is a Greek accusative, 'Butes the champion'. 'Immani corpore' is an ablative of quality. 'Qui se… ferebat' is 'who carried himself', 'who gave himself out', with 'veniens… de gente' 'coming from the race'; 'Bebrycia' agrees with 'gente': the Bebrycians were the people of King Amycus, the boxer who challenged every stranger. 'Moribundum' is 'dying'; 'fulva' is 'tawny'.

sentences.t:
Talis prima Dares caput altum in proelia tollit,
ostenditque umeros latos, alternaque iactat
brachia protendens, et verberat ictibus auras.
sentences.l:
Such first Dares his head high into battles lifts,
and shows shoulders broad, and alternately tosses
arms stretching out, and lashes with blows the air.
sentences.i: Such is Dares as he first raises his lofty head for the fight, shows his broad shoulders, flings his arms out in turn, and thrashes the air with his blows.
sentences.n: 'Talis' is 'such (a man)'; 'prima' is a neuter plural used as an adverb, 'first'. 'In proelia' is 'for the combats'. 'Alterna' is an adjective doing the work of an adverb, 'in turn'. 'Protendens' is 'stretching out'. 'Verberat ictibus auras' is 'lashes the air with blows', shadow-boxing.

sentences.t: Quaeritur huic alius;
sentences.l: Is sought for him another;
sentences.i: A rival for him is sought;
sentences.n: 'Quaeritur' is a passive, 'is sought', and 'alius' is the subject, 'another (man)'. 'Huic' is a dative of the one for whom the search is made.

sentences.t:
nec quisquam ex agmine tanto
audet adire virum manibusque inducere caestus.
sentences.l:
and no one out of so great a crowd
dares to approach the man and on his hands to draw the gloves.
sentences.i: and no man from all that throng dares to go up to him and draw the gloves over his hands.
sentences.n: 'Agmine' is a crowd, here the whole gathered company. 'Adire virum' is 'go up to the man' ('virum' is an accusative singular). 'Manibus inducere caestus' is 'to draw the boxing-gloves on his hands': a 'caestus' is a leather strap loaded with metal, wound round the fist and forearm.

sentences.t:
Ergo alacris, cunctosque putans excedere palma,
Aeneae stetit ante pedes, nec plura moratus
tum laeva taurum cornu tenet, atque ita fatur:
sentences.l:
So eager, and all thinking to give up the palm,
before Aeneas' feet he stood, and no more delaying
then by the left horn the bull he holds, and thus speaks:
sentences.i: Eager, then, and reckoning that all were giving up the palm, he stood before Aeneas's feet, and, without more delay, he grasps the bull by its left horn and speaks:
sentences.n: 'Alacris' is an older form of the nominative, 'eager' (Greenough keeps it). 'Cunctos putans excedere palma' is 'thinking that all withdraw from the palm' ('excedere', with the ablative, 'give up', 'quit'), an accusative and infinitive. 'Aeneae… ante pedes' puts the genitive before the preposition. 'Moratus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'moror', 'having delayed', with 'plura' an accusative of extent, 'any more'. 'Laeva… cornu' is 'by the left horn', with 'laeva' agreeing with 'cornu', and the bull is the prize: he claims it by taking hold of it. 'Fatur' is the deponent 'for', 'speaks'.

sentences.t:
“Nate dea, si nemo audet se credere pugnae,
quae finis standi?
sentences.l:
“Goddess-born, if no one dares himself to trust to the fight,
what end of standing?
sentences.i: “Son of a goddess, if no one dares to commit himself to the fight, what is to be the end of my standing here?
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Dares's speech. 'Nate dea' is 'son of a goddess', with 'nate' the vocative of 'natus' and 'dea' an ablative of origin without a preposition. 'Se credere pugnae' is 'trust himself to the fight'. 'Quae finis standi?' is 'what end of standing?', with 'standi' a gerund (genitive); 'finis' is feminine here.

sentences.t: Quo me decet usque teneri?
sentences.l: Up to what point does it suit me to be held back?
sentences.i: How much longer is it right that I be kept waiting?
sentences.n: 'Quo… usque' is 'how long', separated by 'me decet' (the two parts of 'quousque' apart). 'Decet' is an impersonal verb with the accusative and infinitive: 'me teneri', 'that I be held'.

sentences.t: Ducere dona iube.
sentences.l: To carry off the gifts, bid me.”
sentences.i: Give the word, and let me carry off the prizes.”
sentences.n: The sense is 'order me to take away the prizes'; 'me' is understood as the object of 'iube' and the subject of 'ducere', which suits livestock, 'to lead away'. Greenough prints the closing mark one space late, 'iube. ”Cuncti', which is a misprint of its position (the speech ends at 'iube'); t is kept as printed, with the mark heading the next unit, and l and i close the speech here by sense.

sentences.t:
”Cuncti simul ore fremebant
Dardanidae, reddique viro promissa iubebant.
sentences.l:
All together with one mouth were roaring
the Trojans, and to be given back to the man the promised things were ordering.
sentences.i: All the Trojans together roared with one voice, and called for what was promised to be handed over to the man.
sentences.n: The mark that stands at the head of this unit in t is the misprinted end of Dares's speech (see the note on 385). 'Dardanidae' is 'sons of Dardanus', the Trojans, a Greek patronymic form. 'Ore' is an ablative, 'with (one) mouth'. 'Reddi… promissa iubebant' is 'ordered the promised things to be given' (a passive infinitive after 'iubeo'; 'promissa' is neuter plural, the prize); 'viro' is a dative.
